reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: A rectocele is a herniation of the anterior rectal wall into the posterior vaginal wall through a weakened rectovaginal septum, most common in parous women
Typical symptoms are obstructed defecation, a sensation of incomplete evacuation, vaginal bulging, and the need for vaginal or perineal digitation to empty the rectum
Small rectoceles are a common incidental finding on imaging in asymptomatic women, so symptoms must correlate with anatomical findings before intervention
Risk factors include vaginal childbirth, chronic straining, ageing with connective-tissue laxity, prior pelvic surgery, and oestrogen deficiency
Defecating proctography or dynamic MRI demonstrates the size, barium trapping, and associated pelvic-floor abnormalities such as enterocele or intussusception
Rectocele frequently coexists with other pelvic-floor disorders, so a global structural and functional assessment is essential rather than treating it in isolation
First-line treatment is conservative: fibre, stool softening, avoidance of straining, and biofeedback/pelvic-floor physiotherapy
Surgical repair (transvaginal, transperineal, transanal, or as part of a ventral rectopexy or stapled procedure) is reserved for significant symptomatic rectoceles with demonstrable contrast trapping
reference.pathophysiology: The rectovaginal septum is a fibromuscular layer that separates the rectum from the vagina and supports the anterior rectal wall. Weakening or disruption of this septum and its fascial attachments, most often following vaginal delivery, chronic straining, ageing, or oestrogen deficiency, allows the anterior rectal wall to bulge forward into the posterior vaginal lumen during defecation. As intrarectal pressure rises with straining, stool preferentially fills the outpouching rather than passing through the anal canal, producing trapping of stool, a sensation of incomplete evacuation, and a vicious cycle of increased straining that enlarges the defect. Associated pelvic-floor weakness, perineal descent, and coexisting prolapse of other compartments compound the functional obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Enterocele or sigmoidocele herniating into the rectovaginal space
Rectal intussusception or internal rectal prolapse
Anismus (paradoxical puborectalis contraction) causing obstructed defecation
Cystocele or uterine/vault prolapse contributing to pelvic-floor symptoms
Anterior mucosal or full-thickness rectal prolapse
additionalInvestigations: Defecating proctography to assess rectocele size and barium trapping
Dynamic pelvic-floor MRI to evaluate all three compartments
Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion testing for evacuatory function
Endoanal ultrasound if sphincter injury or incontinence is suspected
Colonic transit studies where slow-transit constipation is considered
Examination in the lithotomy and standing positions with straining
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or change in bowel habit suggesting neoplasia
A non-reducing or ulcerated prolapsing mass
New-onset faecal incontinence or a suspected sphincter defect
Symptoms disproportionate to a small rectocele, prompting search for another cause
Signs of coexisting enterocele obstructing the small bowel
reference.prognosis: Many symptomatic rectoceles improve substantially with conservative measures and biofeedback; surgical repair of well-selected patients with demonstrable contrast trapping gives good functional results, though recurrence and persistent evacuatory symptoms can occur, particularly when other pelvic-floor abnormalities are unaddressed.
pitfalls: Operating on an incidental rectocele that does not correlate with the patient's symptoms
Overlooking coexisting enterocele, intussusception, or anismus that will limit surgical benefit
Failing to treat constipation and straining, leading to recurrence
Attributing obstructed defecation solely to the rectocele when a functional disorder predominates
Neglecting pelvic-floor physiotherapy before considering surgery
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
International Continence Society and International Urogynecological Association terminology and guidance on pelvic organ prolapse
Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland guidance on obstructed defecation
management: First-line conservative management with dietary fibre, fluids, stool softeners and bowel-habit modification to reduce straining
Pelvic-floor physiotherapy and biofeedback to improve rectal evacuation
Vaginal pessary support and topical oestrogen where oestrogen deficiency contributes
Reserve surgical repair (transvaginal, transanal or transperineal) for symptomatic patients with demonstrable contrast trapping after conservative failure
Confirm that symptoms correlate with anatomy before intervention, as small rectoceles are common incidental findings
Multidisciplinary assessment of all pelvic-floor compartments and coexisting enterocele or intussusception, with monitoring for recurrence and persistent evacuatory symptoms
